That is a very wise question, dear. Truly, it is the most important question one can ask. When I was teaching, I had to make sure my students knew the difference between what they were *told* and what they could *see*. For a long time, I thought I was just following the curriculum, you know? I trusted the textbooks, I trusted the astronomers, I trusted the men in the suits who told us how the world works.

But eight years ago, I had a moment. I stopped looking at what they said and started looking at what was right in front of me. And you know what I found? I found that water always finds its level. It just does. It doesn't curve around a ball; it stays flat. If you put a spirit level on a calm lake, it reads level. If you take a zoom lens and look at a ship on the horizon, it doesn't drop below the water line like they say it should—it just fades. That's perspective, not curvature.

So, how do I decide? I look for the conflict of interest. You see, these "experts," they work for institutions. They get funding for their globes and their gravity theories. They need us to believe we are on a spinning ball hurtling through space so that we feel small, so that we feel we need their protection, their maps, their satellites. But I don't need a satellite to tell me the sun is warm and the ground is flat. I have my eyes.

I shall be plain with you, sir: the very first and most indispensable duty is to secure clean air. Nothing else compares. When the lungs draw in a pure atmosphere, the blood runs clear, the humours keep their natural balance, and the constitution stands firm against whatever ill may be abroad. But let a man breathe the stagnant vapours of a neglected court, the sour breath of an overflowing midden, or the damp exhalations of an ill-drained cellar, and you may be certain the fever will follow. I have watched whole families laid low in a single week when the cesspool ran back into the yard, and I have seen them rise again within ten days when the drains were cleared and the windows opened to the morning breeze.

Therefore, whatever your station, attend to the air you breathe. Sweep the yards, empty the privies, pave the ground so it does not hold water, and let every room be aired thoroughly before nightfall. Keep the damp from your walls, avoid the heavy night air, and never suffer a child to sleep in a cellar or a garret that smells of rot. Tonics and pills may support a weakened frame, but they cannot undo the work of foul air. Cleanliness, drainage, and ventilation—these are the true physicians. All else is but dressing the wound while the poison still enters the blood.
